q: Which statement about quality and grade is correct?
options: Low grade is always a problem
Low quality is always a problem; low grade may be acceptable
Quality and grade mean the same thing
explanation: Quality is the degree to which requirements are met. Grade is a category of features. A simple product that works as promised is low grade but good quality.

q: What does "prevention over inspection" mean?
options: Defects should be found by the customer
Quality should be planned and built in, because preventing defects costs less than finding and fixing them
Only the final product needs to be checked
explanation: Quality is built into processes and deliverables. The cost of preventing mistakes is generally much lower than the cost of correcting them after they are found.

q: An independent team from the PMO reviews whether the project is following the organization's quality procedures. What is this?
explanation: A quality audit is a structured, independent process to determine whether activities comply with policies, processes and procedures. It is a quality assurance technique.

q: A team member examines a finished component to check that it conforms to the documented standard. What is this?
explanation: An inspection is the examination of a work product to determine whether it conforms to documented standards. It is a quality control technique.

q: Which tool helps a team trace a problem back to its root cause by branching possible causes off a problem statement?
explanation: A cause-and-effect diagram, also called a fishbone or Ishikawa diagram, breaks the causes of a problem into branches to find the main or root cause.

q: Which tool is used to determine whether a process is stable and has predictable performance?
explanation: Control charts show whether a process is stable, using statistically calculated upper and lower control limits.

q: What is the difference between control limits and specification limits?
options: Control limits are calculated from the process; specification limits come from the requirements
Specification limits are calculated statistically; control limits come from the customer
Control limits apply only to cost
explanation: Specification limits reflect the maximum and minimum values allowed by the requirements. Control limits are determined statistically and show the natural capability of a stable process.

q: On a control chart, seven consecutive points fall above the mean, all within the control limits. What does this indicate?
options: Nothing at all; only points outside the control limits ever matter
The process is out of control and should be investigated
explanation: The rule of seven: seven points in a row on one side of the mean indicate a non-random cause, so the process is considered out of control even inside the limits.
ref: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 7, Q22; PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Control charts

links.label: The Project Management Answer Book, Chapter 7, Q22

q: A team wants to know which few causes are responsible for most of the defects. Which tool should it use?
explanation: A Pareto chart ranks causes from most to least frequent, showing the vital few. It reflects the 80/20 principle: about 80% of problems come from 20% of causes.

q: What is the purpose of a make-or-buy analysis?
options: To decide whether work is best done by the project team or purchased from outside
explanation: A make-or-buy analysis determines whether work or deliverables can best be accomplished by the project team or should be purchased from outside sources.

q: The buyer has a complex requirement and wants sellers to propose how they would solve it. Which bid document should be used?
explanation: An RFP is used for a complex scope where the buyer wants the vendor to provide a solution. An RFQ is used when price is the main factor; an RFI gathers information.

q: The buyer needs 200 standard laptops and price is the main deciding factor. Which bid document fits best?
explanation: An RFQ is used when price is the main deciding factor and the proposed solution is readily available.

q: What is the purpose of a bidder conference?
options: To answer sellers' questions so that all bidders have the same information
To negotiate the price with the preferred seller
explanation: After the bid documents are distributed, the buyer holds a bidder conference to respond to bidder questions and provide clarifying information to all.

q: Only one supplier holds the patent for a required component. Which selection method applies?
explanation: Single-source procurement is used when only one supplier can satisfy the technical requirements, for example because of patents or exclusive rights.

q: In which type of contract does the seller carry most of the cost risk?
explanation: A fixed-price contract sets a predetermined fee for a clearly defined scope, transferring cost risk to the seller and giving the buyer budget predictability.

q: A research project has an uncertain scope. Which contract type is most suitable, and who carries the cost risk?
explanation: Cost-reimbursable contracts pay the seller's actual costs plus a fee. They are used when scope is uncertain or the project is high risk, and the buyer carries the risk of cost escalation.

q: A company hires two consultants at an hourly rate for a task whose scope is not yet clear. Which contract type is this?
explanation: A time and materials contract pays for the actual time and materials used at agreed rates. It is a hybrid, often used for smaller jobs or when scope is unclear.

q: The scope of work is clearly and completely defined and is not expected to change. Which contract type is the buyer most likely to prefer?
explanation: With a well-defined scope the work can be estimated accurately, so a fixed-price contract gives the buyer budget certainty.

q: A dispute arises with a seller over the cost of a change. What should be tried first?
explanation: Negotiation, direct discussion between the parties without a third party, is the first step. Litigation is the last option when all other means are exhausted.

q: In which dispute resolution method does a neutral third party hear both sides and make a binding decision?
explanation: In arbitration an arbitrator or panel hears both sides and makes a binding decision. In mediation the third party only facilitates the parties' own agreement.

q: Why is procurement not a separate performance domain in the 8th edition?
options: Because project procurement is usually integrated into the organization's procurement department and its established processes
Because procurement is only for agile projects
Because contracts are not legally binding
explanation: Project procurements typically extend from the organization's procurement department, using its processes, policies and vendor relationships. The topic is covered in Appendix X4.

q: Which document describes how the team will acquire goods and services from outside the performing organization?
explanation: The procurement management plan is a component of the project management plan that describes how goods and services will be acquired from outside the organization.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Procurement management plan

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Procurement management plan

q: A shaft must be 50 mm thick, plus or minus 0.2 mm. Every shaft measured is inside that range, but the last eight readings have all been above the mean on the control chart. What does this show?
options: All is well, because every shaft measured so far is inside the tolerance that was specified
The tolerance in the requirement was set too wide
The process may be out of control, although the shafts are within tolerance
The control limits and the tolerance are the same thing
explanation: Tolerance is the acceptable variation for the quality requirement. Control limits describe the variation expected from the process. A run of seven or more points on one side of the mean signals a process out of control even when each result is within tolerance.
ref: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, Glossary (Tolerance)

links.label: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, Glossary (Tolerance)

q: A factory produces 5,000 circuit boards for a project. Testing destroys a board, so the quality team tests 50 chosen at random and judges the batch from them. Which technique is this?
explanation: Statistical sampling is choosing part of a population of interest for inspection. It is used when inspecting every item would be too costly or would destroy the product.
ref: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, Glossary (Statistical Sampling)

links.label: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, Glossary (Statistical Sampling)

q: A project needs 200 standard office chairs. The specification is fixed, and the only open question is the price. Which procurement document should go to the sellers?
explanation: A request for quotation asks prospective sellers for prices for common or standard products or services. A request for proposal asks for a proposed solution; a request for information asks about products or seller capability.
ref: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, Glossary (Request for Quotation)

links.label: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, Glossary (Request for Quotation)

q: A project manager is writing the quality management plan and wants to state the basic principles the company follows on quality. Where do these come from?
options: From the project team's own preferences
explanation: The quality policy is set by the organization: it establishes the basic principles that govern the organization's actions as it implements its system for quality management. The project's quality management plan applies it.
ref: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, Glossary (Quality Policy)

links.label: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, Glossary (Quality Policy)

q: During design, engineers follow a set of guidelines whose single aim is to make the product quick to assemble on the line. Which quality tool from the process guide is this?
explanation: Design for X (DfX) is a set of technical guidelines applied during the design of a product to optimize a specific aspect. The X can be reliability, deployment, assembly, manufacturing, cost, service, usability, safety or quality.
ref: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, section 10, Design for X

links.label: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, section 10, Design for X

q: While planning, a software team decides that the product will go through an alpha test with staff and a beta test with fifty customers before release. What does the process guide call this planning activity?
explanation: In test and inspection planning the project manager and team determine, during planning, how to test or inspect the product. The tests depend on the industry: alpha and beta tests in software, strength tests in construction, field tests in engineering.
ref: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, section 10, Test and inspection planning

links.label: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, section 10, Test and inspection planning

q: Five sellers reply to a request for proposal. Before comparing prices, the buyer's team checks that each reply is complete and answers every part of the bid documents and the statement of work. Which tool is this?
explanation: Proposals are evaluated to ensure they are complete and respond in full to the bid documents, the procurement statement of work, the source selection criteria and any other documents in the bid package.
ref: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, section 10, Proposal evaluation

links.label: Process Groups: A Practice Guide, section 10, Proposal evaluation

q: Match each description with the way of settling a claim or dispute.
left: The parties talk directly, with no third party
A neutral third party helps them reach their own agreement
A neutral third party hears both sides and gives a binding decision
explanation: Negotiation is always tried first and litigation is the last option. A mediator helps the parties agree; an arbitrator decides for them, and the decision binds.

q: Match each description with the contract type.
left: A set price for a clearly defined scope
The seller's actual costs plus a fee
Agreed rates for the hours and materials used
Savings and overruns against an agreed figure are shared
explanation: Fixed-price suits a well-defined scope. Cost-reimbursable suits uncertain or high-risk work. Time and materials is a hybrid, used for smaller jobs or staff augmentation. Target-cost rewards efficiency on large projects.

q: Every part is within the customer's tolerance. Select the one sample that nevertheless shows the process is out of control.
explanation: Sample 4 lies above the upper control limit, although it is inside the tolerance. A point outside a control limit means the process is out of control and the cause should be investigated. Control limits come from the process; the tolerance comes from the requirement.

q: No sample in these three groups is outside a control limit. Select the group that still signals a process out of control.
explanation: Samples 8 to 14 are seven points in a row on the same side of the mean. This is the rule of seven: the process is out of control even though every point is within the control limits.

q: Which method have they chosen?

strip.says: We have talked for a month and still cannot agree on your claim.
Then let us bring in a neutral person to help us find a settlement of our own.
Agreed, as long as nothing that person says binds us.

explanation: In mediation a neutral third party helps the parties reach their own agreement. In arbitration the third party makes a binding decision. Negotiation, which they have already tried, has no third party.
